claim: Increased genomic instability is one of the hallmarks of cancer.
source: One of the hallmarks of cancer is increased genomic instability (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011

claim: Over-expression of oncogenes have been shown to induce genomic instability.
source: In addition to DNA replication errors and /or mutations induced by exposure to DNA damaging agents, over-expression of oncogenes have been shown to induce genomic instability (Bartkova et al., 2005; Gorgoulis et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bartkova et al., 2005 and Gorgoulis et al., 2005

claim: Myc is mutated or over-expressed in multiple types of cancer.
source: As one of the most widely studied oncogenes in cancer biology, it is mutated or over-expressed in multiple types of cancer (Pelengaris et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pelengaris et al., 2002

claim: Myc is involved in driving cellular proliferation and promoting stem cell self-renewal under normal circumstances.
source: Myc is involved in driving cellular proliferation and promoting stem cell self-renewal under normal circumstances.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about Myc function

claim: When myc is overexpressed in a cell, it can cause increased genomic instability and promote carcinogenesis.
source: When myc is overexpressed in a cell, it can cause increased genomic instability and promote carcinogenesis (Karlsson et al., 2003; Ray et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Karlsson et al., 2003 and Ray et al., 2006

claim: Several studies suggest that myc-induced genomic instability and carcinogenesis is a result of an overabundance of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Several studies suggest that myc-induced genomic instability and carcinogenesis is a result of an overabundance of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Vafa et al., 2002; Felsher and Bishop, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vafa et al., 2002 and Felsher and Bishop, 1999

claim: Myc overexpression can cause DNA damage and transformation in the absence of ROS.
source: However, it has also been reported that myc overexpression can cause DNA damage and transformation in the absence of ROS (Ray et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ray et al., 2006

claim: Over-expression of myc has been shown to induce apoptosis.
source: Over-expression of myc has been shown to induce apoptosis (Evan et al., 1992; Harrington et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Evan et al., 1992 and Harrington et al., 1994

claim: Apoptosis has been widely recognized as an anti-carcinogenic process based on the assumption that it is utilized by the host to eliminate damaged cells.
source: Until recently, apoptosis has been widely recognized as an anti-carcinogenic process based on the assumption that it is utilized by the host to eliminate damaged cells, including those suffering DNA damage (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Reed, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011 and Reed, 1999

claim: There has been increasing evidence that apoptosis may in fact been involved in promoting carcinogenesis.
source: However, there has been increasing evidence that apoptosis may in fact been involved in promoting carcinogenesis (Tang et al., 2012; Ichim et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tang et al., 2012, Ichim et al., 2015, and Liu et al., 2015

claim: Mammalian cells exposed to external stress can survive activation of the apoptotic cascade and incur increased genetic instability and oncogenic transformation.
source: Mammalian cells exposed to external stress can survive activation of the apoptotic cascade and incur increased genetic instability and oncogenic transformation.
evidence: Statement based on prior research findings

claim: Mammalian cells that survive apoptosis experience increased mitochondria membrane permeability (MOMP).
source: Studies show that mammalian cells that survive apoptosis experience increased mitochondria membrane permeability (MOMP)(Ichim et al., 2015) and sublethal caspase 3 activation (Liu et al., 2015), which lead to activation of downstream endonucleases such as CAD and endoG, which in turn cause increased genetic instability and oncogenic transformation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ichim et al., 2015

claim: Mammalian cells that survive apoptosis experience sublethal caspase 3 activation.
source: Studies show that mammalian cells that survive apoptosis experience increased mitochondria membrane permeability (MOMP)(Ichim et al., 2015) and sublethal caspase 3 activation (Liu et al., 2015), which lead to activation of downstream endonucleases such as CAD and endoG, which in turn cause increased genetic instability and oncogenic transformation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2015

claim: Sublethal caspase 3 activation leads to activation of downstream endonucleases such as CAD and endoG.
source: Studies show that mammalian cells that survive apoptosis experience increased mitochondria membrane permeability (MOMP)(Ichim et al., 2015) and sublethal caspase 3 activation (Liu et al., 2015), which lead to activation of downstream endonucleases such as CAD and endoG, which in turn cause increased genetic instability and oncogenic transformation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ichim et al., 2015 and Liu et al., 2015

claim: Activation of downstream endonucleases such as CAD and endoG cause increased genetic instability and oncogenic transformation.
source: Studies show that mammalian cells that survive apoptosis experience increased mitochondria membrane permeability (MOMP)(Ichim et al., 2015) and sublethal caspase 3 activation (Liu et al., 2015), which lead to activation of downstream endonucleases such as CAD and endoG, which in turn cause increased genetic instability and oncogenic transformation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ichim et al., 2015 and Liu et al., 2015

claim: Sublethal activation of caspase 3 and endonuclease G plays an essential role in Myc-induced genetic instability and oncogenic transformation in human cells.
source: We show sublethal activation of caspase 3 and endonuclease G plays an essential role in Myc-induced genetic instability and oncogenic transformation in human cells.
evidence: Main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Mammalian cells exposed to external stress such radiation and chemicals could survive the activation of apoptotic caspases.
source: Previously, we and others have shown that mammalian cells exposed to external stress such radiation and chemicals could survive the activation of apoptotic caspases.
evidence: Reference to prior research findings

claim: Among the cells that survive caspase activation, elevated DNA damage, such as DNA double strand breaks were observed.
source: Among the cells that survive caspase activation, elevated DNA damage, such as DNA double strand breaks were observed.
evidence: Reference to prior research findings

claim: Myc over-expression in mammalian cells promotes caspase activation and cell death.
source: Our hypothesis is based on the well-established evidence that Myc over-expression in mammalian cells promotes caspase activation and cell death (Karlsson et al., 2003; Ray et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Karlsson et al., 2003 and Ray et al., 2006

claim: MCF10A is an immortalized but not transformed human mammary epithelial cell line.
source: To investigate the effects of Myc expression we used a recombinant lentivirus to transduce the c-Myc gene under the control of a constitutively active CMV promoter into MCF10A cells, an immortalized but not transformed human mammary epithelial cell line (Soule et al., 1990; Tait et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to Soule et al., 1990 and Tait et al., 1990

claim: Roughly 6% of Myc-expressing MCF10A cells were observed with having relatively normal nuclei and cleaved caspase 3.
source: Roughly 6% of Myc-expressing MCF10A cells were observed with having relatively normal nuclei and cleaved caspase 3, as compared to control MCF10A cells where only ~1% of the cells were observed with cleaved caspase 3.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: Control MCF10A cells have only ~1% of the cells observed with cleaved caspase 3.
source: Roughly 6% of Myc-expressing MCF10A cells were observed with having relatively normal nuclei and cleaved caspase 3, as compared to control MCF10A cells where only ~1% of the cells were observed with cleaved caspase 3.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: Irrespective of Casp3 activation status in the presence or absence of Myc expression, 40% or more of the individually sorted MCF10A cells can form colonies in 96-well plates.
source: Our data indicate that irrespective of Casp3 activation status in the presence or absence of Myc expression, 40% or more of the individually sorted MCF10A cells can form colonies in 96-well plates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Despite increased Casp3EGFP activities in Myc-expressing MCF10A cells, the levels of Annexin V staining did not increase significantly.
source: Further flow cytometry analysis showed that despite increased Casp3EGFP activities in Myc-expressing MCF10A cells, the levels of Annexin V staining, a well-recognized marker of apoptosis, did not increase significantly (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: A significant fraction of MCF10A cells can survive spontaneous or Myc-induced Casp3 activation.
source: Those data provide clear evidence that a significant fraction of MCF10A cells can survive spontaneous or Myc-induced Casp3 activation.
evidence: Inference from experimental data on colony formation and Annexin V staining

claim: Myc overexpression caused significant increases in both the fraction of cells with and the average numbers per cell of γH2AX foci and chromosomal aberrations in control MCF10A cells.
source: In control MCF10A cells, Myc overexpression caused significant increases in both the fraction of cells with and the average numbers per cell of γH2AX foci and chromosomal aberrations (Figure 1D–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D–G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Myc overexpression in Casp3-deficient cells induced no increases in the numbers of either chromosome aberrations or γH2AX foci when compared to control MCF10A or CASP3 knockout (CASP3KO) cells without Myc overexpression.
source: In contrast, Myc overexpression in Casp3-deficient cells induced no increases in the numbers of either chromosome aberrations or γH2AX foci when compared to control MCF10A or CASP3 knockout (CASP3KO) cells without Myc overexpression (Figure 1D–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D–G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: c-Myc expression was not homogeneous, perhaps a reflection of the silencing of the CMV promoter that controlled c-Myc expression.
source: Our results indicate that c-Myc expression was not homogeneous, perhaps a reflection of the silencing of the CMV promoter that controlled c-Myc expression.
evidence: Observation from immunofluorescence data with speculative interpretation

claim: γH2AX foci presence did not always correlate with high c-Myc expression, perhaps indicating a stochastic nature of γH2AX foci induction.
source: Furthermore, γH2AX foci presence did not always correlate with high c-Myc expression, perhaps indicating a stochastic nature of γH2AX foci induction.
evidence: Observation from immunofluorescence data with speculative interpretation

claim: Myc expression caused not only higher background levels of γH2AX foci but also higher residual foci levels after a significant number of the induced foci were repaired.
source: A systematic analysis on the repair of radiation-induced γH2AX foci showed that Myc expression caused not only higher background levels of γH2AX foci but also higher residual foci levels after a significant number of the induced foci were repaired.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5

claim: CASP3 knockout eliminated most of the basal and residual levels of γH2AX foci in MCF10A cells.
source: On the other hand, CASP3 knockout eliminated most of the basal and residual levels of γH2AX foci in MCF10A cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5

claim: Casp3 re-expression restored Myc-induced DNA damage foci in CASP3KO MCF10A cells.
source: Our results indicate that Casp3 re-expression restored Myc-induced DNA damage foci (Figure 1—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6B

claim: DnCasp3 differs from wild-type Casp3 in only a single amino acid that eliminates its cleavage activities.
source: DnCasp3 differs from wild-type Casp3 in only a single amino acid that eliminates its cleavage activities (Stennicke and Salvesen, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stennicke and Salvesen, 1997

claim: dnCASP3 re-expression did not restore the ability of Myc to induce γH2AX foci.
source: In contrast to wild-type Casp3 re-expression, dnCASP3 re-expression did not restore the ability of Myc to induce γH2AX foci (Figure 1—figure supplement 6C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6C

claim: Myc overexpression resulted in statistically significant increases in γH2AX foci in BJ1 cells.
source: Similar to MCF10A cells, we observed that Myc overexpression resulted in statistically significant increases in γH2AX foci (Figure 1—figure supplement 7B) and chromosomal aberrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 7C) in cells overexpressing Myc.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7B

claim: Myc overexpression resulted in statistically significant increases in chromosomal aberrations in BJ1 cells.
source: Similar to MCF10A cells, we observed that Myc overexpression resulted in statistically significant increases in γH2AX foci (Figure 1—figure supplement 7B) and chromosomal aberrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 7C) in cells overexpressing Myc.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7C

claim: Myc-induced increases in γH2AX foci and chromosomal aberrations were almost completely eliminated in CASP3KO BJ1 cells.
source: However, such increases were almost completely eliminated in CASP3KO BJ1 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 7B,C), similar to CASP3KO MCF10A cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7B,C

claim: Myc overexpression in control MCF10A resulted in a significant increase in the number of observed soft agar colonies.
source: Our results indicate that Myc overexpression in control MCF10A resulted in a significant increase in the number of observed soft agar colonies (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B

claim: Myc-induced increases in soft agar colonies were completely absent in Casp3 knockout cells.
source: However, such increases were completely absent in Casp3 knockout cells (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B

claim: In Casp3KO cells with Casp3 re-expression, the ability of Myc to induce soft agar colony formation was restored.
source: The causative role for Casp3 in this process was further demonstrated in Casp3KO cells with Casp3 re-expression, the ability of Myc to induce soft agar colony formation was restored (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: In control MCF10A cells, expression of an exogenous Casp3 caused no increase in Myc-induced soft agar colony formation.
source: In control MCF10A cells, expression of an exogenous Casp3 caused no increase in Myc-induced soft agar colony formation (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Only the group of nude mice that were injected with Myc-transduced control MCF10A cell were able to form tumors after 8 weeks of observation.
source: Despite injection of 4 × 106 cells each, only the group of nude mice that were injected with Myc-transduced control MCF10A cell were able to form tumors after 8 weeks of observation (Figure 2D), thereby confirming that both Myc over-expression and an intact CAPSP3 gene are required for oncogenic transformation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Both Myc over-expression and an intact CAPSP3 gene are required for oncogenic transformation.
source: Despite injection of 4 × 106 cells each, only the group of nude mice that were injected with Myc-transduced control MCF10A cell were able to form tumors after 8 weeks of observation (Figure 2D), thereby confirming that both Myc over-expression and an intact CAPSP3 gene are required for oncogenic transformation.
evidence: Inference from experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: In Myc over-expressing MCF10A cells, five out of eight injected sites formed tumors.
source: A more detailed examination showed that in Myc over-expressing MCF10A cells, five out of eight injected sites formed tumors, albeit with varying growth kinetics (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Casp3 deficiency completely blocked the ability of Myc to transform MCF10A cells in vivo.
source: The in vivo data here are striking in that Casp3 deficiency completely blocked the ability of Myc to transform MCF10A cells.
evidence: Inference from experimental data on tumor formation in nude mice

claim: Casp3 deficiency significantly reduced Myc-induced soft agar colony formation in vitro, but it was not completely blocked.
source: In vitro, although Casp3 deficiency significantly reduced Myc-induced soft agar colony formation, it was not completely blocked.
evidence: Inference from experimental data on soft agar colony formation

claim: Endonuclease G (endo G) is an apoptotic endonuclease that normally resides within the mitochondria and migrates to the nucleus after activation of apoptotic cascade.
source: In a previous study, endonuclease G (endo G), an apoptotic endonuclease that normally resides within the mitochondria and migrates to the nucleus after activation of apoptotic cascade (Parrish et al., 2001; Li et al., 2001), is responsible for much of the Casp3-induced genomic instability after stress exposure.
evidence: Supported by citations to Parrish et al., 2001 and Li et al., 2001

claim: EndoG is responsible for much of the Casp3-induced genomic instability after stress exposure.
source: In a previous study, endonuclease G (endo G), an apoptotic endonuclease that normally resides within the mitochondria and migrates to the nucleus after activation of apoptotic cascade (Parrish et al., 2001; Li et al., 2001), is responsible for much of the Casp3-induced genomic instability after stress exposure.
evidence: Reference to prior research findings with citations to Parrish et al., 2001 and Li et al., 2001

claim: There was a significant increase in the fraction of cells with endoG nuclear migration in Myc-expressing MCF10A vs control cells (11% vs 2%).
source: Our results show that there was a significant increase in the fraction of cells with endoG nuclear migration in Myc-expressing MCF10A vs control cells (11% vs 2%, Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B

claim: The increase in endoG nuclear migration was completely eliminated in CASP3 knockout cells.
source: However, the increase was completely eliminated in CASP3 knockout cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: ENDOG deletion was able to eliminate both Myc-induced γH2AX foci.
source: Our results show that ENDOG deletion was able to eliminate both Myc-induced γH2AX foci (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and oncogenic transformation as evaluated by use of the soft agar colony-forming assay (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: ENDOG deletion was able to eliminate Myc-induced oncogenic transformation as evaluated by use of the soft agar colony-forming assay.
source: Our results show that ENDOG deletion was able to eliminate both Myc-induced γH2AX foci (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and oncogenic transformation as evaluated by use of the soft agar colony-forming assay (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: CASP3KO caused small reductions in both Annexin V+ and Annexin V+/PI+ MCF10A cells when compared with control cells.
source: Our results (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) indicate that CASP3KO caused small reductions in both Annexin V+ and Annexin V+/PI+ MCF10A cells when compared with control cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: ENDOG knockout caused small increases in fractions of Annexin V+/PI- and Annexin V-/PI+ cells when compared with control cells.
source: However, ENDOG knockout caused small increases in fractions of Annexin V+/PI- and Annexin V-/PI+ cells when compared with control cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Myc expression caused increases in fractions of Annexin V+/PI+ cells in all three cell populations.
source: Myc expression, on the other hand, caused increases in fractions of Annexin V+/PI+ cells I all three cell populations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: CASP3 or ENDOG knockout caused small increase and decrease in MCF10A cells, respectively.
source: Our results indicate that CASP3 or ENDOG knockout caused small increase and decrease in MCF10A cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, top panels), respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Forced MYC expression increased ROS in wild-type MCF10A cells but not in CASP3KO or ENDOGKO MCF10A cells.
source: Forced MYC expression increased ROS in wild-type MCF10A cells but not in CASP3KO or ENDOGKO MCF10A cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, mid-panels).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Myc was able to induce significantly more ROS in wild-type MCF10A cells than CASP3KO cells.
source: Further, Myc was able to induce significantly more ROS in wild-type MCF10A cells than CASP3KO cells, but about equal levels of ROS in wild type vs ENDOGKO cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, lower panels).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Myc was able to induce about equal levels of ROS in wild type vs ENDOGKO cells.
source: Further, Myc was able to induce significantly more ROS in wild-type MCF10A cells than CASP3KO cells, but about equal levels of ROS in wild type vs ENDOGKO cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, lower panels).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Although ROS production appeared to track with carcinogenesis in wild-type and CASP3KO cells, it did not in ENDOGKO cells.
source: Those data suggest that although ROS production appeared to track with carcinogenesis in wild-type and CASP3KO cells, it did not in ENDOGKO cells.
evidence: Inference from experimental data on ROS levels

claim: MYC expression in MCF10A cells caused a significant increase in cytoplasmic mtDNA levels.
source: Our results indicate that MYC expression in MCF10A cells caused a significant increase in cytoplasmic mtDNA levels, indicating that a significant fraction of mitochondria had compromised membrane integrity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: A significant fraction of mitochondria had compromised membrane integrity in MYC-expressing MCF10A cells.
source: Our results indicate that MYC expression in MCF10A cells caused a significant increase in cytoplasmic mtDNA levels, indicating that a significant fraction of mitochondria had compromised membrane integrity.
evidence: Inference from experimental data on cytoplasmic mtDNA levels

claim: CASP3KO significantly reduced cytoplasmic mtDNA levels in MCF10A cells with or without Myc over expression.
source: On the other hand, CASP3KO significantly reduced cytoplasmic mtDNA levels in MCF10A cells with or without Myc over expression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: Casp3 and other upstream factors that promote mitochondrial leakage form a positive loop to promote mitochondrial leakage with or without Myc expression.
source: While we are not clear of the exact cause of this, we speculate that Casp3 and other upstream factors that promote mitochondrial leakage form a positive loop to promote mitochondrial leakage with or without Myc expression.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental data

claim: NLS-endoG expression restored the depleted γH2AX foci induction by Myc in CASO3KO cells.
source: Our results indicate the NLS-endoG expression restored the depleted γH2AX foci induction by Myc in CASO3KO cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: NLS-endoG alone was sufficient to induce γH2X foci in CASP3KO cells to levels induced by Myc.
source: In fact, NLS-endoG alone was sufficient to induce γH2X foci in CASP3KO cells to levels induced by Myc (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: NLS-EndoG restored the ability of Myc to induce oncogenic transformation in Casp3 knockout MCF10A cells.
source: Our results show that NLS-EndoG restored the ability of Myc to induce oncogenic transformation in Casp3 knockout MCF10A cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E

claim: NLS-EndoG expression alone was not sufficient to induce oncogenic transformation despite its ability to induce DNA damage foci to levels similar to Myc expression.
source: However, NLS-EndoG expression alone was not sufficient to induce oncogenic transformation despite its ability to induce DNA damage foci to levels similar to Myc expression (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E

claim: While endoG nuclear migration is a necessary condition for Myc-induced oncogenic transformation, it is not sufficient by itself.
source: Those results suggest while endoG nuclear migration is a necessary condition for Myc-induced oncogenic transformation, it is not sufficient by itself.
evidence: Inference from experimental data on NLS-EndoG effects

claim: Additional activities of Myc are clearly required in the transformation process.
source: Additional activities of Myc are clearly required in the transformation process.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing NLS-EndoG alone is insufficient for transformation

claim: NLS-EndoG restored the ability of Myc to induce oncogenic transformation in CASP3KO MCF10A cells in nude mice.
source: NLS-EndoG restored the ability of Myc to induce oncogenic transformation in CASP3KO MCF10A cells (Figure 4F), with five out of eight inoculations formed tumors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Five out of eight inoculations of CASP3KO MCF10A cells with NLS-EndoG and Myc formed tumors in nude mice.
source: NLS-EndoG restored the ability of Myc to induce oncogenic transformation in CASP3KO MCF10A cells (Figure 4F), with five out of eight inoculations formed tumors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F

claim: NLS-EndoG alone was not able to make MCF10A cells with CASP3 gene knockout to become tumorigenic.
source: On the other hand, NLS-EndoG alone was not able to make MCF10A cells with CASP3 gene knockout to become tumorigenic, consistent with results from soft agar colony formation assay (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F

claim: The present study provides significant new insights into the roles of Myc in carcinogenesis.
source: The present study provides significant new insights into the roles of Myc in carcinogenesis.
evidence: Summary statement of the study's contribution

claim: The study resolves two apparently paradoxical observations regarding Myc: its ability to stimulate apoptosis and to induce genomic instability and oncogenic transformation.
source: In particular, it resolves two apparently paradoxical observations regarding Myc: its ability to stimulate apoptosis and to induce genomic instability and oncogenic transformation.
evidence: Summary statement of the study's contribution

claim: In the case of Myc, the apoptotic machinery is exploited by Myc as a vehicle to cause genomic instability and induce oncogenic transformation.
source: However, in the case of Myc, the apoptotic machinery, is exploited by Myc as a vehicle to cause genomic instability and induce oncogenic transformation.

claim: Casp3 and Endo G, two well-established apoptosis effectors, are activated and required for Myc-induced oncogenic transformation.
source: Most strikingly, our data suggest that Casp3 and Endo G, two well-established apoptosis effectors, are activated and required for Myc-induced oncogenic transformation.

claim: Myc-induced activation of apoptosis is actually part and parcel of Myc's capacity to induce mammalian transformation.
source: This finding suggest that Myc-induced activation of apoptosis, instead of being a result of Myc induced cellular stress, is actually part and parcel of Myc's capacity to induce mammalian transformation.

claim: It is possible that deregulation in mitochondrial biogenesis, which is known to be stimulated by Myc, may be responsible for Myc-induced mitochondrial leakage and Casp3 activation.
source: While we do not have any experimental evidence at present, it is possible that deregulation in mitochondrial biogenesis, which is known to be stimulated by Myc, may be responsible for it, as suggested previously (Dang et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2007; Ahuja et al., 2010).

claim: The discovery is consistent with an increasing body of literature that suggest a pro-oncogenic role for apoptosis and some apoptotic factors.

claim: Cells exposed to stress can survive caspase activation.

claim: The observation of cells surviving caspase activation in development, chemical exposure, and radiation exposure indicate that it is a wide spread phenomenon.

claim: The observation of cells surviving Myc-induced caspase activation is a significant extension of earlier observations.
source: Our observation of cells surviving Myc-induced caspase activation is a significant extension of those earlier observations and may provide important insights into the relationship between apoptosis and oncogene-induced transformation beyond that of Myc.

claim: Casp3 and endo G, two key factors in the canonical apoptosis pathway, play essential, facilitative roles in Myc-induced oncogenic transformation.
source: Taken together, our study provides crucial evidence that Casp3 and endo G, two key factors in the canonical apoptosis pathway, play essential, facilitative roles in Myc-induced oncogenic transformation.

claim: Endonuclease G, an apoptotic nuclease downstream of Caspase-3, is directly responsible for Myc-induced genetic instability.

claim: Caspase-3 plays a critical, unexpected role in mediating Myc-induced genetic instability and transformation in mammalian cells.
